title: ZESTRIL (lisinopril) tablets, for oral use: full prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration-approved labelling, published in DailyMed (National Library of Medicine); structured product label version 2, effective 2 January 2025, label text revised 11/2024
funder: not stated. The document is prescribing information approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and published by the labeller, Upsher-Smith Laboratories, LLC.
result: Initial US approval 1988. Indications: hypertension in adults and in children of 6 years and older, adjunct therapy for systolic heart failure, and reduction of mortality in haemodynamically stable patients within 24 hours of acute myocardial infarction. Boxed warning, fetal toxicity: when pregnancy is detected, discontinue as soon as possible; drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus; use during the second and third trimesters reduces fetal renal function and increases fetal and neonatal morbidity and death, and the resulting oligohydramnios can be associated with fetal lung hypoplasia and skeletal deformations, including skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension and renal failure. Mechanism: ACE is a peptidyl dipeptidase that catalyses the conversion of angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, which also stimulates adrenal aldosterone secretion; inhibition lowers plasma angiotensin II, vasopressor activity and aldosterone secretion, which may raise serum potassium slightly; removal of angiotensin II negative feedback raises plasma renin activity; ACE is identical to kininase, the enzyme that degrades bradykinin, and whether raised bradykinin plays a part in the therapeutic effect remains to be elucidated; the drug is antihypertensive even in low-renin hypertension, and Black patients had a smaller average response to monotherapy. In hypertensive patients with normal renal function treated for up to 24 weeks, mean serum potassium rose by about 0.1 mEq/l, with increases above 0.5 mEq/l in about 15% and decreases above 0.5 mEq/l in about 6%. Hyperkalaemia (serum potassium above 5.7 mEq/l) occurred in 2.2% of treated patients with hypertension and 4.8% with heart failure; risk factors are renal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus and concomitant potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes. Pharmacokinetics: peak serum concentrations at about 7 hours; food does not alter bioavailability; mean extent of absorption about 25% from urinary recovery, with large intersubject variability of 6% to 60%; lisinopril does not undergo metabolism and is excreted unchanged entirely in the urine; effective half-life on multiple dosing 12 hours; the prolonged terminal phase probably represents saturable binding to ACE; absolute bioavailability falls to 16% in stable NYHA class II to IV heart failure; elimination is little changed above a glomerular filtration rate of 30 ml/min; removable by haemodialysis. Dosing in renal impairment: half the usual initial dose at creatinine clearance of 10 to 30 ml/min, and 2.5 mg once daily below 10 ml/min or on haemodialysis. Adverse reactions exceeding placebo by 2% in hypertension: headache by 3.8%, dizziness by 3.5%, cough by 2.5%; 5.7% of patients discontinued for adverse reactions. ATLAS trial, high against low dose: dizziness 19% against 12%, hypotension 11% against 7%, creatinine increased 10% against 7%, hyperkalaemia 6% against 4%, syncope 7% against 5%. Angio-oedema of the face, extremities, lips, tongue, glottis or larynx, including fatal reactions, has occurred at any time during treatment; ACE inhibitors have been associated with a higher rate of angio-oedema in Black than in non-Black patients; intestinal angio-oedema has occurred with normal C1 esterase levels; previous angio-oedema or hypersensitivity on an ACE inhibitor, and hereditary or idiopathic angio-oedema, are contraindications, as is combination with a neprilysin inhibitor such as sacubitril or, in diabetes, with aliskiren. GISSI-3: 19,394 patients within 24 hours of acute myocardial infarction, randomised in a 2 by 2 factorial design to six weeks of lisinopril, nitrates, both or open control; patients receiving lisinopril (n=9646) had an 11% lower risk of death at six weeks than those who did not (n=9672), 6.4% against 7.2% (p=0.04), with persistent hypotension in 9.0% against 3.7% and renal dysfunction in 2.4% against 1.1%. Dual blockade of the renin-angiotensin system with an angiotensin receptor blocker, an ACE inhibitor or aliskiren raises the risks of hypotension, hyperkalaemia and changes in renal function; in VA NEPHRON-D, 1448 patients with type 2 diabetes, raised urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio and reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate were randomised to lisinopril or placebo on a background of losartan and followed for a median 2.2 years; the combination gave no additional benefit for decline in GFR, end-stage renal disease or death, and increased hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury. Abrupt withdrawal has not been associated with a rapid increase in blood pressure or with a significant increase compared with pretreatment levels. Patients are told to report immediately any sign suggesting angio-oedema and to take no more of the drug until they have consulted the prescribing physician, and not to use potassium-containing salt substitutes without consulting their physician.
